q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: SELECT b.name AS bar_name, COALESCE(drinker_counts.total_num_drinker, 0) AS total_num_drinker, COALESCE(beer_prices.avg_price, NULL) AS avg_price, COALESCE(most_regular.most_reg_drinker, NULL) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN (SELECT f.bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS total_num_drinker FROM frequents AS f GROUP BY f.bar) AS drinker_counts ON b.name = drinker_counts.bar LEFT JOIN (SELECT s.bar, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price FROM serves AS s GROUP BY s.bar) AS beer_prices ON b.name = beer_prices.bar LEFT JOIN (SELECT f.bar, f.drinker AS most_reg_drinker FROM frequents AS f INNER JOIN (SELECT bar, MAX(times_a_week) AS max_times FROM frequents GROUP BY bar) AS max_frequent ON f.bar = max_frequent.bar AND f.times_a_week = max_frequent.max_times ORDER BY f.bar, f.drinker) AS most_regular ON b.name = most_regular.bar ORDER BY total_num_drinker DESC, bar_name

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because of the way they handle the subquery for the most regular drinker. Q1 orders the subquery by times_a_week DESC and drinker ASC, while Q2 orders by bar and drinker. This can lead to different results if there are multiple drinkers with the same number of times_a_week.
counterexample_dsp: Create a scenario with two bars, each having two drinkers with the same number of times_a_week, but different drinker names. The order of drinker names should be different between the two bars to trigger the difference.
